steps.body:
Welcome back. You can wrangle lists now, and here is a nice payoff: a string is basically a sequence of characters, so a lot of what you learned about lists works on text too.

You can index and slice a string the same way. word[0] is the first character, word[-1] is the last, len(word) is how many characters, and word[0:3] slices out the first three. Same brackets, same counting-from-0.

One crucial difference we will keep coming back to: a string is IMMUTABLE. You cannot change a character in place. But you can build brand new strings from old ones endlessly, and that is exactly what all the string tools do.

steps.prompt: Run this. Index, slice, and length, just like a list.
Slice out positions 1 and 2 (stop before 3). What prints?

steps.body:
Strings carry a toolbox of methods, called with a dot. The everyday ones:
.upper() and .lower() change the case: "Hi".upper() is "HI".
.strip() trims whitespace off both ends, a lifesaver for cleaning up typed input with stray spaces.
.replace(old, new) swaps every occurrence of one piece of text for another.

Here is the habit to build: every one of these hands you back a NEW string and leaves the original untouched (strings are immutable, remember). So you catch the result in a variable: clean = raw.strip(). You can also chain them left to right: raw.strip().lower() trims, then lowercases the trimmed result.

steps.prompt: Run this. Trim, then trim-and-lowercase, then a replace.
steps.code:
raw = "  Hello World  "
print(raw.strip())
print(raw.strip().lower())
print("cat dog cat".replace("cat", "fish"))

steps.body:
Two methods handle the bridge between one string and a list of strings, and you will use them constantly.

.split() breaks a string into a list, cutting at each space by default, or at whatever separator you pass: "a,b,c".split(",") gives ["a", "b", "c"]. This is how you pull apart a line of data.

.join() is the reverse: it glues a list of strings back into one string, with a separator of your choice between them. ", ".join(["a", "b"]) gives "a, b". Read it as: the separator string does the joining. A little backwards at first, but it clicks fast.

split to take text apart, join to put it back together.

steps.prompt: Run this. Split a line into pieces, then join the pieces a new way.
steps.code:
line = "niko,coding,games"
parts = line.split(",")
print(parts)
print(" and ".join(parts))

steps.body:
Now the confusion that immutability causes, because it produces a very specific bug.

You cannot change a character in place: word[0] = "X" raises an error. Instead, every string method returns a brand new string and leaves the original alone. So a line like raw.strip() all by itself does nothing useful: it builds a trimmed string and then throws it away because you did not catch it. You have to assign the result: raw = raw.strip(). Forgetting to catch it is one of the most common beginner string bugs, and now you will spot it instantly.

To check whether a piece of text appears inside a string, the cleanest tool is in: "cat" in "category" is True. Simple and readable.

steps.prompt: in checks whether the left text appears inside the right. What prints?
You wrote raw.strip() on its own line to clean up raw, but afterward raw STILL has its spaces. Why?
choices: strip() returns a NEW string; you have to catch it, like raw = raw.strip().
strip() only removes spaces from the middle of the text.
strip() needs you to pass it an argument.
Strings cannot be stripped at all.

reviewForm.expected: Strings are immutable, so strip() returns a new string instead of changing raw. You must catch it: raw = raw.strip().

steps.prompt: This is supposed to return the text trimmed and lowercased, but it returns it exactly as it came in. The bug is the immutability trap: strip() and lower() build new strings that are being thrown away. Catch the results.
steps.starterCode:
def tidy(text):
    text.strip()
    text.lower()
    return text

steps.body: Little text transformers are some of the most satisfying quick programs to write, and they show up everywhere (usernames, slugs, filenames). Let us build one, combining lower, split, and join into a single function.

boss.name: The Text Refinery
boss.taunt: Messy in, tidy out. Take this sloppy input and make it presentable.
boss.brief:
Real input is always messy: extra spaces, wrong case, inconsistent separators. Your job is to clean it up. Write two text tools.

1. clean_tags(raw): the input is a comma-separated string of tags with random spacing and casing. Return a LIST of the tags, each trimmed of spaces and lowercased. Split on commas, then strip and lower each piece.
   Example: clean_tags("Python, Coding ,GAMES") returns ["python", "coding", "games"].

2. headline(text): trim the text and title-case it (capitalize the first letter of each word). The .title() method does the capitalizing.
   Example: headline("  the daily log  ") returns "The Daily Log".

This is the whole module working together: split, strip, lower, title, a loop, and append, all aimed at turning a mess into something clean.

each piece must be stripped of its surrounding spaces and lowercased

terms.definition: Trims whitespace off both ends of a string and returns the new, trimmed string. Essential for cleaning up typed input.
Swaps every occurrence of one piece of text for another, returning a new string. "cat cat".replace("cat", "dog") gives "dog dog".
Breaks a string into a list of pieces, cutting at spaces by default or at a separator you pass. "a,b".split(",") gives ["a", "b"].
Glues a list of strings into one string, with a chosen separator between them. "-".join(["a", "b"]) gives "a-b". The separator does the joining.
Cannot be changed in place. Strings are immutable, so every string method returns a NEW string. You must catch the result: raw = raw.strip().
Checks whether one piece of text appears inside another. "cat" in "category" is True. The cleanest way to test for a substring.
